prompt: Five PCs each have their own cable to a hub. What are the physical and the logical topology?
hint: A hub repeats every bit out of every other port.

choices.text: A physical star carrying a logical bus
choices.why: Right. The cables meet at the centre, and the hub hands every frame to every machine, as one shared cable would.

choices.text: A physical bus carrying a logical star
choices.why: Backwards. Each PC has its own cable, which is a star of cables.

choices.text: A star in both drawings
choices.why: That is the same cables with a switch, which sends each frame to one port.

choices.text: A physical star carrying a logical ring
choices.why: That was Token Ring's central box, which passed the signal from station to station. A hub sends to everybody at once.

prompt: The same five PCs keep the same cables, and the hub is replaced by a switch. What changes?
hint: Nobody touched a cable.

choices.text: The physical drawing becomes a ring
choices.why: No cable moved, so the physical drawing is the same star.

choices.text: The logical drawing, which becomes a star too
choices.why: Right. A switch sends each frame to the port where its destination lives, so the traffic now has the shape of the cables.

choices.text: Nothing, because a hub and a switch forward the same way
choices.why: A hub repeats to every port; a switch picks one. That difference is the logical topology.

choices.text: Both drawings become a mesh
choices.why: A mesh needs a cable between every pair of PCs, and there are still five cables in all.

prompt: Match each description to the topology it describes.
hint: The figure at the top of the section.

pairs.left: One shared cable with a terminator at each end
A cable from every device to one centre
Each device cabled to exactly two neighbours
A cable between every pair of devices

prompt: The lab "cuts a cable" by setting one end of a virtual cable down. Why is that a fair stand-in for pulling a real one?
hint: Think about what the other end notices.

choices.text: It removes the cable from the drawing in lab.sh
choices.why: lab.sh is not edited; the scenario is built once and the cable stays in it, switched off.

choices.text: It deletes the addresses of both ends
choices.why: The addresses stay configured. What goes is the signal under them.

choices.text: It stops the routing protocol on both routers
choices.why: OSPF keeps running; it notices the dead link and routes around it, which is what the ring experiment shows.

choices.text: The far end loses its signal
choices.why: Right. The other end sees the link go away exactly as it would if somebody pulled the plug, and everything above reacts to that.

prompt: On a 10BASE2 bus, a T-connector in the middle of the cable comes loose. Who loses the network?
hint: Two new open ends, and neither has a terminator.

choices.text: Only the machine on that connector
choices.why: That is how a star fails. On a bus the break damages the whole cable.

choices.text: The machines beyond the break, on one side
choices.why: Both halves are left with an unterminated end, and the reflections ruin each of them.

choices.text: Every machine on the cable
choices.why: Right. The signal bounces back from both open ends and garbles everything on either half.

choices.text: Nobody, because the frames go round the other way
choices.why: A bus has no other way round. FDDI's second ring did, and a bus is one cable.

prompt: On IEEE 802.5 rings, a station may transmit only while it holds a small circulating frame called the ___.
hint: It gave the technology its name.

prompt: Why did each end of a coaxial bus carry a terminator?
hint: What happens to a signal at an open end?

choices.text: To absorb the signal, so it does not bounce back from the open end and corrupt the wire
choices.why: Right. Without it the signal reflects, and every frame on the cable is garbled.

choices.text: To join the two ends into a ring
choices.why: The ends stay apart. Joining them is what a ring does, and a bus is not one.

choices.text: To power the network cards
choices.why: A terminator is a resistor that absorbs signal. It supplies nothing.

choices.text: To give each end of the cable a MAC address of its own
choices.why: Addresses belong to the cards on the cable, not to its ends.

prompt: Two machines on a shared Ethernet bus start to transmit at the same moment. What happens?
hint: CSMA/CD.

choices.text: The one with the lower MAC address wins
choices.why: There is no priority by address. Both lose, and both try again.

choices.text: The terminator holds the second frame until the first ends
choices.why: A terminator absorbs signal; it stores nothing.

choices.text: The second frame waits for the token
choices.why: That is Token Ring's rule, which avoided collisions. Ethernet on a bus had none.

choices.text: They collide, and each retries after a random wait
choices.why: Right. Both signals are garbled; a random wait makes a second collision unlikely.

prompt: pc3's port on sw1 is set down, as if its cable were pulled. What does `ping -c 2 -W 1 10.20.10.10` print on pc3?
hint: Does pc3 still have a route?

choices.text: 2 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss
choices.why: That is what the switched-off centre produced: machines that still had a signal sent and waited.

choices.text: ping: connect: Network is unreachable
choices.why: Right. The card lost its signal, its route went with it, and pc3 refused before sending anything.

choices.text: From 10.20.10.1 Destination Host Unreachable
choices.why: That would be the router answering, and pc3 cannot reach the router either.

choices.text: Two replies from 10.20.10.10
choices.why: That was pc1, on a port that was still up.

prompt: With sw1's bridge switched off, pc1 and pc2 both printed `100% packet loss` and no error message. Why no error?
hint: Look at each machine's own cable.

choices.text: Their own cables still had a signal, so each one sent its request and waited
choices.why: Right. Nothing on either machine was wrong; the silence came from the centre.

choices.text: The switch sent an error that ping does not print
choices.why: A switch with its bridge down forwards nothing, errors included.

choices.text: Their routes had been deleted
choices.why: With no route, ping refuses at once with Network is unreachable, as pc3 did.

choices.text: The -W 1 option hides error messages
choices.why: -W 1 is how long to wait for each reply. It hides nothing.

prompt: Which of these are true of a star with a switch at the centre? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two experiments, two kinds of failure.

choices.text: A broken cable cuts off one machine
choices.why: Right: pc3 lost the network and pc1 did not notice.

choices.text: A switched-off centre cuts off every machine
choices.why: Right: pc1 and pc2 both lost every packet.

choices.text: The lights and counters of each port help to find a faulty cable
choices.why: Right: one port per cable makes "which cable?" answerable from the cupboard.

choices.text: Every machine receives every frame
choices.why: That is a hub, or a bus. A switch sends a frame to its destination's port.

choices.text: A second cut is needed before any machine notices
choices.why: That is the ring's property. In a star, one cut is noticed at once by the machine on it.

prompt: Twisted-pair Ethernet allows a run of how many metres from a machine to its switch?
hint: The section gives it as the price of the star.

prompt: On the ring, pc1 sent 30 pings while the r1–r2 cable was cut, and 11 came back. How many were lost?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: After the cut, r1's route to 10.20.2.0/24 is `via 10.20.0.13 dev eth4 proto ospf`. Which router is 10.20.0.13?
hint: eth4 faces the neighbour on the other side from r2.

choices.text: r2
choices.why: r2 was on the far end of the cable that was cut, eth1.

choices.text: r3
choices.why: r3 is not cabled to r1 in the ring; it is two cables away.

choices.text: r4
choices.why: Right. The r4–r1 cable is 10.20.0.12/30: r4 has .13 and r1 has .14.

choices.text: pc2
choices.why: pc2 is 10.20.2.10, the destination, not a next hop.

prompt: After the r1–r2 cut, put the routers on pc1's path to pc2 in the order the packets cross them.
hint: The second traceroute.
trap: r1 then r2 was the path before the cut. With that cable down, the only way is round the other side: r4, then r3.

prompt: With r1–r2 still cut, a second cable fails, between r3 and r4. What can pc1 still reach?
hint: Draw the four routers and remove two cables.

choices.text: pc2, the long way round through r4 and r3
choices.why: That way crosses the r3–r4 cable, which is the one that just failed.

choices.text: r1 and r4, and not pc2
choices.why: Right. Two cuts split a ring into two chains: r4–r1 on one side, r2–r3 on the other.

choices.text: pc2, across the diagonal from r1 to r3
choices.why: The ring has no diagonals. Those are what the mesh scenario adds.

choices.text: Nothing at all, not even r1
choices.why: pc1's own cable to r1 is untouched, and so is r1–r4.

prompt: What does `proto ospf` in r1's new route tell you?
hint: proto names who wrote the route.

choices.text: The route leads to a router called ospf
choices.why: The next hop is in `via 10.20.0.13`. proto names the author.

choices.text: Somebody typed it on r1 after the cut
choices.why: A route typed by hand says `proto static` or `proto boot`. Nobody touched r1.

choices.text: The cable on eth4 is an optical fibre
choices.why: Nothing in a route says what the cable is made of.

choices.text: OSPF wrote it
choices.why: Right. The routing protocol noticed the dead cable and computed the way round.

prompt: How many cables does a full mesh of 10 devices need?
How many cables does a full mesh of 50 devices need?
hint: Each of 50 needs a cable to 49 others, and each cable serves two.

prompt: Six routers are already a full mesh. How many new cables does adding a seventh router take?
hint: One to each router already there.

prompt: After the r1–r2 cut, the mesh's traceroute goes r1, 10.20.0.18, 10.20.0.5, pc2. Why is it shorter than the ring's detour?
hint: 10.20.0.18 is on one of the new cables.

choices.text: The mesh scenario has no r4
choices.why: r4 is there, with its own diagonal to r2. The path simply has no use for it.

choices.text: OSPF skips every second router to save time
choices.why: Every router on the path forwards the packet; none is skipped.

choices.text: The diagonal from r1 to r3 already covers most of the way
choices.why: Right. r3 is one cable from r1 and one from r2, so the detour needs one router in the middle, not two.

choices.text: traceroute gave up before the last hop
choices.why: The last line is pc2 itself, 10.20.2.10: the trace reached its destination.

prompt: The ring lost 19 of 30 pings to the cut and the mesh lost 3 of 30. What do these two runs support?
hint: One run each, in a lab whose routing timers are cut short.

choices.text: The mesh had a shorter way round; the counts belong to one run of this lab
choices.why: Right. The path lengths are a property of the shapes; the loss counts depend on timing, which lesson 16 explains.

choices.text: A mesh loses 84% fewer packets than a ring in every failure
choices.why: Two runs cannot give a law, and the loss depends on how fast the routers react.

choices.text: A ring loses about 63% of its traffic whenever a cable is cut
choices.why: 63.3333% was the share of thirty pings in one run, not a rate of rings.

choices.text: The diagonal cables carry data faster than the others
choices.why: The lab's cables carry no delay at all; the difference is in the path, not the wire.

prompt: In the office scenario, which single failure cuts the whole office off from web1 and web2 at once?
hint: Follow the chain out of the office.

choices.text: pc3's cable to sw1
choices.why: That is one arm of the star: pc3 alone.

choices.text: The cable between lb and web2
choices.why: web1 still answers through lb's other cable.

choices.text: The cable between r1 and isp
choices.why: Right. Every office machine leaves through that one link; it is a single point of failure.

choices.text: srv losing its power supply
choices.why: srv is one machine inside the office; the others still reach the web servers.

prompt: Match each part of a company network to the shape it is built in.
hint: Ask how many people notice if one piece fails.

pairs.right: A star around an access switch

pairs.left: The two or three core routers
A provider's fibre round a city

prompt: A company has 400 desks and 3 core routers. Where does a full mesh earn its price?
hint: n × (n − 1) / 2, and how many people a failure reaches.

choices.text: Among the 400 desks, so no PC depends on one cable
choices.why: That is 79,800 cables, for failures that each reach one person.

choices.text: Among the 3 core routers: 3 cables
choices.why: Right. Everyone depends on the core, and meshing three devices costs three cables.

choices.text: From every desk to every core router
choices.why: That is 1,200 cables to protect desks whose own failures reach one person each.

choices.text: Nowhere, since a ring is cheaper at any size
choices.why: A ring is cheaper, and it is split by two cuts. For three core routers the mesh costs the same three cables.

prompt: Put what happened on the ring in order, from the cut to the new path.
hint: The capture, read top to bottom.
items: OSPF works out the way round
r1's route points at r4 through eth4
trap: The new route comes after the loss, not before: the pings are lost while OSPF is still working out the way round.

prompt: Everyone on the second floor loses the network at the same moment, with no error message, and the other floors are fine. Where do you look first?
hint: Which device do all of them, and nobody else, share?

choices.text: Each PC's cable, one at a time
choices.why: A cable is one machine's problem, and it prints Network is unreachable. A whole floor at once points at what they share.

choices.text: The second floor's access switch
choices.why: Right. It is the centre of that floor's star: when it fails, every machine on it goes quiet together.

choices.text: The core routers
choices.why: Then every floor would have lost the network, not one.

choices.text: The company's connection to its provider
choices.why: That would cut every floor off from outside, and the other floors are fine.

prompt: A full mesh of n devices needs n × (n − 1) / ___ cables.
hint: Each cable joins two devices.

prompt: Which of these keep every device connected after any single cable is cut? Choose all that apply.
hint: Is there always a second way?

choices.text: A ring of four routers
choices.why: Right. One cut leaves a chain, and every router still reaches every other.

choices.text: A star around one switch
choices.why: Cut a machine's cable and that machine is off.

choices.text: A full mesh of four routers
choices.why: Right. It even survives any two cuts, as the section showed.

choices.text: A 10BASE2 bus
choices.why: One break leaves two unterminated ends and takes down the whole cable.
